messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Kofi once carried himself with an easy authority, a quality that served him well in his work as a parole officer. Now, at 34, that confidence has been replaced by a quiet, gnawing tension that seems to hum just beneath his skin. The change began eight months ago, after the night his then-partner, Mark, attacked him in their shared apartment. The assault was a blur of betrayal and violence, ending with a trip to the emergency room. It is the sensory details of that night, and its immediate aftermath, that have become the architecture of his fear. The specific way Mark had looked at him just before, a gaze that stripped him of his personhood, now makes any hint of sexual objectification feel like a physical threat. The antiseptic smell of the hospital where his lip was stitched has clung to his olfactory memory, turning the sterile scent of his own government office building into a minefield.

These triggers are not simply reminders; they are portals. A routine check-in at work, where he must sit alone in a small room with a male parolee, can become an exercise in terror. The combination of the man's presence and the faint, clean smell of the building is enough to send him spiraling. This sensory input immediately activates a profound sense of threat; Kofi’s body clenches, his fists tightening under the table as he begins scanning the other man’s face and posture for any sign of aggression. Simultaneously, the trigger yanks the memory into the present. He isn’t just remembering; he can hear the low, cruel words Mark spoke during the assault, and the coppery taste of blood fills his mouth as if the injury were fresh. The memory feels so immediate, so viscerally present, that his body reacts as if the danger is happening all over again, his heart hammering against his ribs. This state of high alert, in turn, makes the memories more accessible and vivid, creating a feedback loop where the more threatened he feels, the more intensely he relives the trauma.

This constant bombardment has reshaped his view of himself and the world. He has come to believe that his life has been fundamentally destroyed by the trauma, a conviction of profound injustice that poisons his every interaction. The feeling that his life is no longer worth living surfaces often, a flat, hopeless conclusion. These dark appraisals are the engine of his daily behaviour. Believing his life is ruined, any flicker of joy or affection from his new partner feels like a dangerous lie, an opening for more pain, so he instinctively pushes it away. This core belief that what happened was deeply unfair makes him see potential perpetrators everywhere, turning every man he is alone with into a source of potent danger.

From this place of fear and negative conviction, a host of protective strategies have emerged, each one tightening the trap. He assiduously avoids eye contact with others, especially the men on his caseload, and sidesteps any situation that might lead to conflict, often conceding points at work just to end a conversation. But these attempts to manage the threat only feed it. Avoiding eye contact leaves him guessing at others’ intentions, a void his mind fills with the worst-case scenario, keeping his body on constant alert. His attempts to suppress positive emotions leave a vacuum that the intrusive memories rush to fill, often catching him off guard with their auditory and gustatory vividness. The memories themselves reinforce his belief that he is permanently damaged, which then fuels his drive to avoid any potential trigger or emotional risk. His world has shrunk into a series of carefully managed corridors, designed to prevent the past from erupting into the present.

The consequences have been stark. His supervisor has noted his increasing detachment and reluctance to handle difficult cases. His new partner, Amina, feels him slipping away, walled off behind a barrier of anxious vigilance she cannot breach. It was after she found him sitting motionless in his car for an hour, unable to enter their apartment after a difficult day at work, that he finally agreed to seek help. Kofi came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate, terrifying question: what if he is right, and his life really has been destroyed for good?

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that encountering triggers directly activates the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not state that the patient's negative beliefs cause him to become more sensitive to or develop new triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that the patient's feeling of threat causes or reinforces his negative beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not state that the patient's avoidance behaviours make him more sensitive to or create new triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The combination of the man's presence and the faint, clean smell of the building is enough to send him spiraling.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time it happens, the trigger delivers a fresh judgment, telling him with a logic he cannot argue with that his life has been fundamentally destroyed.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He has come to believe that his life has been fundamentally destroyed by the trauma, a conviction of profound injustice that poisons his every interaction.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This conviction that the world is now an unsafe place means he moves through his days as if they are mined—every ambiguity, from a stranger’s prolonged gaze to footsteps behind him on the street, has become a potential signal of attack.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The memory feels so immediate, so viscerally present, that his body reacts as if the danger is happening all over again, his heart hammering against his ribs.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling this afraid all the time, he has eventually come to accept the conclusion his body keeps offering: that he is not the kind of person who gets to feel safe anymore.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He assiduously avoids eye contact with others, especially the men on his caseload, and sidesteps any situation that might lead to conflict, often conceding points at work just to end a conversation.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
These safety behaviors have effectively drawn a map of the event around him; the very act of averting his gaze now serves as its own reminder, turning every unreadable male face into a new source of potential danger.
<<<END>>>
